voiceover: How early did Christians worship Jesus as God? Astonishingly early — and the evidence comes from long before any council ever wrote it down. Start with a hostile witness. Around the year 112, the Roman governor Pliny wrote to his emperor about the Christians he was executing, and reported their strange habit: they met before dawn to sing a hymn 'to Christ, as to a god.' A pagan official, no friend of the faith — describing worship of Jesus within about eighty years of the cross. Go earlier. Around the year 107, Ignatius, a bishop being marched to the arena to die, writes plainly of 'Jesus Christ our God.' No argument, no apology — just the settled speech of his churches. Earlier still, the first Aramaic-speaking Christians prayed 'marana tha' — 'Our Lord, come!' — a prayer addressed to Jesus. And it was never Jesus only. From the beginning the church baptized 'in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,' and praised the three together. Around the year 210, Tertullian had already put it in Latin: three persons, one substance — the Trinity. The historian Larry Hurtado, studying this not as an apologist but as a scholar, called the rise of the worship of Jesus a 'big bang': explosively rapid, erupting in the earliest years after the cross. The worship came first. The definitions came later, to guard what the church had prayed all along.
